target: AG1’s claim that AI can make everyday life more enjoyable and convenient, improve work and school outcomes, increase accessibility, and improve workplace safety overall.
objection: AI is harmful overall because it tends to automate away tasks, destabilize labor markets and existing business practices, undermine critical thinking, repeat and exacerbate racism, and create dangerous privacy risks.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s economic harms mean it reduces societal well-being.
objection: AI can also raise productivity and enable useful new services and tools, improving economic well-being rather than only reducing it.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking in education and work.
objection: AI does not necessarily weaken critical thinking; when used as interactive, explainable assistance that encourages users to check and refine ideas, it can support or even strengthen critical thinking.

target: AG2’s claim that AI inevitably worsens racial inequality and harms racial minorities.
objection: Racially biased outcomes are not unavoidable, because AI systems can be tested for disparate impact, improved with better training data, and governed with ongoing human oversight to reduce racial harms.

target: AG2’s claim that AI inherently increases privacy risks.
objection: Privacy harms can be reduced through data minimization, access controls, and privacy-preserving system design, so AI can be deployed in ways that protect privacy instead of increasing risk.

target: AG1’s claim that fairness safeguards and privacy-preserving design can remove AI’s racial and privacy harms.
objection: Those safeguards are not reliably sufficient in practice across changing contexts and large-scale deployment, so discrimination and privacy invasion can persist despite them.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is not good unless all harms are eliminated.
objection: Whether AI is good should be judged by net effects on well-being, so AI can still be good even if some fairness and privacy harms remain.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms outweigh its benefits because it weakens critical thinking and privacy.
objection: AI can produce concrete well-being gains through workplace safety and health, and through disability accessibility and inclusion, which can outweigh the harms claimed.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be used as guided assistance that strengthens critical thinking in educational settings.
objection: In real educational and work settings, AI often functions as an answer provider under time pressure, so users do not verify or refine ideas themselves and instead rely on AI outputs, which commonly weakens independent critical thinking.

target: AG1’s claim that AI accessibility tools can be deployed in privacy-preserving ways.
objection: Accessibility tools like speech-to-text and vision assistance typically require processing highly sensitive personal data, and large-scale processing and storage of that data creates recurring privacy risks from misuse, breach, or secondary use.

target: AG2’s claim that AI commonly weakens critical thinking in day-to-day settings.
objection: AI educational tools can be designed as interactive tutoring that gives hints and requires learners to generate and justify their own steps, so time pressure does not eliminate the reasoning work needed to strengthen critical thinking.

target: AG2’s claim that AI accessibility tools commonly increase privacy risk.
objection: AI accessibility tools can use privacy-preserving architectures such as on-device or edge processing and minimal data retention, which reduce collection and exposure of sensitive data and therefore protect privacy.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be good for society if deployed in interactive tutoring and privacy-preserving ways.
objection: That pro-AI argument depends on deployment conditions that are not reliably met: typical market incentives favor convenience, engagement, monetized personalization, more data collection, and less reliance on step-by-step tutoring or strict privacy minimization.

target: AG2’s claim that typical market incentives prevent AI from producing net social benefits.
objection: Workplaces and institutions have strong incentives to prevent injuries because accidents create legal and direct costs, so AI workplace-safety tools are more likely to be implemented beneficially than the pessimistic generalization assumes.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms overwhelm its benefits in typical deployments.
objection: AI can improve workplace safety and disability accessibility, and even if some education or privacy conditions are not met everywhere, those other well-being channels can still make the overall impact positive.

target: AG1’s claim that workplace-safety AI reliably yields net benefits.
objection: Workplace AI is often deployed by employers who also want productivity tracking and cost reduction, so the same monitoring infrastructure can become worker surveillance and labor insecurity rather than net safety improvement.

target: AG1’s overall claim that AI’s benefits outweigh its harms.
objection: If workplace AI tends to reduce well-being through surveillance, economic insecurity, and privacy/autonomy harms, then its safety benefits cannot reliably offset the broader harms.

target: AG1’s overall defense of AI as socially beneficial.
objection: AI models are trained on very large datasets that can include personal or identifying information, can leak or reconstruct sensitive data, and can generate realistic synthetic content for deception and misinformation; together these properties make privacy harms hard to eliminate and commonly undermine critical judgment and critical thinking, creating major persistent risks that make AI not good for society.
